Close behind, **Maybe Happy Ending** distinguishes itself as one of Broadway's most original works in recent years, with critics praising the robot love story's unexpected emotional depth and innovation.

The comedy spectrum proves equally strong, with **Oh, Mary!** delivering Cole Escola's absurdist take on Mary Todd Lincoln to rave reviews, while **The Book of Mormon** continues its irreverent satirical run. Meanwhile, spectacular productions like **The Lion King** and **Harry Potter and the Cursed Child** demonstrate Broadway's unmatched capacity for visual storytelling and theatrical magic.

This month's lineup also features the timely **Ragtime** revival, showcasing Joshua Henry's powerhouse performance, and **Hadestown**, the folk-opera that reimagines Greek mythology through inventive staging. Rounding out the selections are **Buena Vista Social Club**'s intoxicating Cuban rhythms, and the enduring appeal of **Chicago**'s cynical entertainment.

With an average critic score of 83/100 across these ten productions, March 2026 represents a particularly strong moment for Broadway, offering theatergoers everything from groundbreaking new voices to reimagined classics. Whether you're drawn to hip-hop history lessons, robot romances, or dazzling spectacle, this month's Broadway lineup rewards both first-time visitors and seasoned theater enthusiasts.

best-broadway-shows-for-kids.intro:

Parents should note that "kid-friendly" encompasses a range of ages and sensibilities—while The Lion King works for nearly all children, Harry Potter's length and darker themes may suit older kids better. Review individual show details to match content and runtime with your family's needs and attention spans.

# Best Broadway Shows from 2020

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway shows that opened in 2020 represent a fascinating snapshot of theater interrupted. That season, cut dramatically short by the pandemic shutdown, nevertheless delivered several productions that continue to resonate with audiences and critics alike.

Leading our rankings is a reimagined **Les Misérables** at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre, earning an 82/100 from critics. This grittier reboot of the beloved musical demonstrates how classic material can be reinvigorated for contemporary audiences, though the approach doesn't win over every reviewer.

**A Soldier's Play** stands out as a particularly significant entry from this truncated season. Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama, making its long-overdue Broadway debut, proves that its examination of race, power, and justice within the military remains urgently relevant. With a 78/100 score across 29 reviews, this stellar revival showcases the enduring power of work that finally found its Broadway moment.

The season's other notable productions include Laura Linney's solo turn in **My Name is Lucy Barton**, which divides critics between those captivated by her luminous performance and those who find the adaptation itself lacking. Meanwhile, Ivo van Hove's radical **West Side Story** reimagining sparked debate with its bold visual approach, exemplifying how even the most iconic musicals can inspire fresh interpretations.

With an average critic score of 74/100 across these five productions, the class of 2020 reflects both Broadway's artistic ambitions and the unpredictable circumstances that would soon reshape the industry entirely. For theatergoers interested in this pivotal moment in Broadway history, these productions offer valuable perspectives on what was—and what might have been.

The season showcased an exceptional range of theatrical voices, from intimate character studies to ambitious meta-theatrical experiments. **Kimberly Akimbo** emerged as a critical darling, earning widespread praise for its delicate balance of humor and heartbreak in telling the story of a teenager with a rare aging condition. **A Strange Loop**, Michael R. Jackson's Pulitzer Prize-winning meta-musical, pushed boundaries with its brutally honest exploration of a Black queer artist's inner life, while the stripped-down revival of **Into the Woods** served as a poignant tribute to Stephen Sondheim, who passed away just months before the production opened. # Best Broadway Plays from 2020

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway plays that opened in 2020 represent a fascinating snapshot of theater interrupted—productions that launched just before or during one of the most turbulent periods in theatrical history. These five shows, now six years into their runs or revivals, continue to generate discussion and demonstrate the resilience of live performance.

Leading the pack is **Les Misérables**, which earns the highest marks at 82/100 for its grittier reboot at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre. This reimagined production proves that even beloved classics can find new life through bold directorial choices, though the approach doesn't win over every traditionalist.

**A Soldier's Play** stands as perhaps the most significant artistic achievement among this group, bringing Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama to Broadway for the first time in a stellar revival that earns 78/100. The production's examination of race, power, and justice within the military resonates powerfully, and critics consistently praise its long-overdue arrival on the Great White Way.

The remaining shows offer varied experiences: Laura Linney commands the stage in the intimate **My Name is Lucy Barton** (71/100), while **Grand Horizons** (71/100) delivers familiar but well-executed boulevard comedy anchored by veteran performers. Ivo van Hove's polarizing **West Side Story** (68/100) reimagining proves the most divisive, with its radical staging choices inspiring both passionate defense and critique.

With an average score of 74/100 across these five productions, the 2020 season offers something for every theatergoer—from traditional revivals to experimental reinventions. Explore the individual reviews to find which production aligns with your theatrical tastes.

# Best Broadway Plays That Opened in 2021

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway plays that debuted in 2021 represent a remarkable period of theatrical innovation and resilience. These productions marked the industry's triumphant return following an unprecedented shutdown, and five years later, their artistic achievements continue to resonate.

The ten highest-rated plays from that year average an impressive 81/100 from critics, reflecting a season of exceptional quality and daring experimentation. Leading the pack is **Dana H.**, Lucas Hnath's unconventional docudrama featuring Deirdre O'Connell's stunning lip-sync performance that critics describe as mesmerizing and unforgettable. Close behind, Rebecca Frecknall's immersive reimagining of **Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club** earns widespread acclaim for its stunning transformation of the Playhouse Theatre into a fully realized nightclub experience.

The season's range is striking—from Andrew Lloyd Webber's enduring spectacle **The Phantom of the Opera** to intimate solo performances like Ruben Santiago-Hudson's virtuosic **Lackawanna Blues**. Epic storytelling arrives through **The Lehman Trilogy**, while **Is This a Room** transforms a verbatim FBI transcript into gripping theater. Marianne Elliott's gender-swapped **Company** revival revitalizes Sondheim's masterwork, and Antoinette Chinonye Nwandu's **Pass Over** served as Broadway's powerful reopening statement. The pop-infused **SIX** and Lynn Nottage's warm **Clyde's** round out a season that balanced entertainment with artistic ambition.

Whether you're discovering these productions for the first time or revisiting theatrical landmarks from a pivotal year, this guide offers insights into the plays that helped define Broadway's renaissance.

From Jordan E. Cooper's provocative satire **Ain't No Mo'** to Paula Vogel's still-relevant **How I Learned to Drive**, these productions reflect theater's capacity to challenge, comfort, and confront audiences with both contemporary urgency and timeless themes. For theatergoers exploring Broadway's current offerings, this collection represents essential viewing from a landmark year in recent theatrical history.

best-broadway-plays-2025.intro:

The season also features several ambitious new works, including Sanaz Toossi's Pulitzer-winning **English**, which explores language and identity with intelligence and sensitivity, and Branden Jacobs-Jenkins' **Purpose**, another characteristically sharp family drama from one of American theater's most vital voices. **Liberation**, Lauren Wohl's feminist memory play, tackles timely themes with strong performances, while **Ragtime** returns to Broadway with Joshua Henry delivering a powerhouse performance in this resonant revival.

With an impressive average critic score of 84/100 across these ten productions, this collection represents some of the strongest theatrical work currently on Broadway stages. Whether you're drawn to classic revivals, new American plays, or innovative family entertainment, this season offers exceptional options worth exploring.

best-broadway-plays-2026.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays of 2026

March 2026 brings a notably lean opening schedule for new Broadway plays, with just one production making its debut this month. While the limited roster reflects the challenging economics facing straight plays on Broadway, the sole entry demonstrates the enduring appeal of well-crafted psychological drama.

**Bug** stands as the month's singular offering, marking the long-awaited Broadway premiere of Tracy Letts' 1996 psychological thriller. With a solid critic score of 74/100 across 35 reviews, the production earns mostly positive notices for its intense exploration of paranoia and delusion. Originally produced by Chicago's Red Orchid Theatre three decades ago, the play arrives on Broadway with renewed relevance, its themes of conspiracy and fractured reality resonating in contemporary discourse. Critics particularly praise the production's claustrophobic staging and committed performances, though some note the material's deliberately unsettling nature may not appeal to all theatergoers.

The sparse March schedule underscores a broader trend in commercial theater, where plays increasingly struggle to secure Broadway berths amid rising production costs and risk-averse producers. That **Bug** makes it to the Great White Way at all speaks to both the strength of Letts' reputation—bolstered by his Pulitzer Prize-winning **August: Osage County**—and the theater community's ongoing commitment to provocative, challenging work.

For audiences seeking substantive dramatic fare this month, **Bug** offers a compelling if confronting option that showcases the raw power of theatrical storytelling. Those planning their spring theater calendar should consider catching this production while monitoring announcements for upcoming play openings in the months ahead.
